title: DHS Algebra 1
text:
Welcome to Algebra 1
Welcome to Algebra 1 at Frederick Douglass High School!
This book will guide you through the most important math skills you’ll need to succeed in high school and beyond. Algebra is more than just solving equations. It’s a powerful way to understand patterns, solve problems, and think logically.
Whether you’re reviewing old ideas or learning something brand new, this book is here to help you every step of the way.

Each unit includes:

We’ll start with the basics (like working with numbers and fractions) and build up to more complex ideas like equations, graphs, and even quadratics.
You don’t have to be a “math person” to do well here. Just bring your curiosity, a little patience, and the willingness to try.
Let’s get started!

title: 1.1 - Integers & Number Lines
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
Did you know that all of mathematics is actually built up from simple things like counting? Even advanced topics like algebra and calculus are just clever ways of organizing and extending basic ideas (like moving forward and backward on a number line).
In this lesson, we’ll use the number line not just to count, but to add, subtract, and compare positive and negative numbers. That might sound basic, but it’s the foundation of nearly everything else you’ll do in Algebra.
Negative numbers can be tricky, especially when the rules don’t always match what your gut tells you. But if you can master the way they work on the number line (including things like opposites, absolute value, and comparison) you’ll be setting yourself up for success in the rest of the course.
Answer as best you can – even if you aren’t sure!

title: 1.2 - Factors, Multiples & Prime Factorization
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
Have you ever had to split something up evenly, like slices of pizza or players on a team? That’s really what factors are about: dividing numbers into equal parts.
In this lesson, you’ll learn how to:
You’ll use these skills again and again, from simplifying fractions to solving equations.

title: 1.3 - GCF & Simplifying Fractions
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
Suppose you’re making snack packs and have 20 bags of chips and 35 cookies. What’s the greatest number of identical packs you can make with no leftovers? To figure that out, you’d use something called the greatest common factor (GCF).
In this lesson, you’ll learn how to use prime factorization to find the GCF, and how that can help you simplify fractions. Finding the GCF makes numbers easier to work with, whether you’re making snack packs or solving math problems.

title: 1.4 - Multiplying & Dividing Fractions
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
In previous lessons, you’ve learned how fractions, decimals, and percents relate to each other. But to solve real-world problems (like adjusting recipes, calculating discounts, or determining grades) you also need to multiply and divide these numbers.
In this lesson, you’ll learn how to multiply and divide fractions and mixed numbers. We’ll explore why multiplying fractions is actually simpler than it seems, and why dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by something called a reciprocal. These skills will help you tackle percent problems and practical applications in upcoming lessons.

title: 1.5 - Adding & Subtracting Fractions
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
In earlier lessons, you learned how to multiply and divide fractions. But many real-world problems, like combining ingredients, measuring distance, or tracking time, require adding and subtracting fractions instead.
In this lesson, you’ll learn how to add and subtract fractions and mixed numbers. We’ll focus on why common denominators matter, how to find them efficiently, and how to avoid common mistakes.

title: 1.6 - Fractions, Decimals & Percents: Conversions
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
Fractions, decimals, and percents are just different ways of showing the same thing (a part of a whole). Whether you’re splitting a pizza, measuring a distance, or shopping during a sale, these numbers are everywhere.
In this lesson, you’ll learn how to move between these forms and understand how they relate to each other. This will be an important skill for solving many types of problems that involve parts of a whole.

title: 1.7 - Solving Problems With Fractions, Decimals & Percents
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
Now that you know how to multiply and divide fractions, you’re ready to apply those skills to real-life problems.
Fractions, decimals, and percents all show parts of a whole, but they’re used in different ways. We see them every day: in grades, prices, sales, surveys, and more.
In this lesson, you’ll practice choosing the right form for the situation, estimating or calculating accurately, and solving common problems like “What percent of this is that?” or “What do I need to score on the test to get an A?”
Use mental math if you can!

title: 1.8 - Order of Operations
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
What does this equal?
\[
6 + 2 \times 3
\]
If you said 24, you’re not alone, but that’s not the correct answer. Math has specific rules for what to do first. These rules are called the order of operations, and they help make sure everyone simplifies expressions the same way.
In this lesson, you’ll learn how to follow those rules correctly, even when negatives, fractions, and grouping symbols are involved.

title: Introduction
text:
What You’ll Learn
Welcome to Unit 2! Here we use variables and expressions to model real situations and simple rules. You’ll learn to read expressions, write them from words, simplify, and evaluate by plugging in values. You’ll also see when two different-looking expressions actually mean the same thing.
By the end of this unit, you’ll be able to:

title: Introduction
text:
Name the parts of an expression (variables, terms, coefficients, constants) and tell what they mean in context.
Translate between words and expressions and choose operations in the correct order (use parentheses when needed).
Evaluate expressions by substitution using the order of operations.
Combine like terms to simplify, and explain why this works (same variable and same power).
Use the distributive property to remove parentheses and simplify; know situations where distribution does not apply (e.g., to exponents).
Describe rules with words, tables, and expressions, and decide if a relation is a function (exactly one output for each input); use function notation as simple shorthand.
Tell whether two expressions are equivalent by simplifying or by substitution, and understand the difference between testing a few values and proving they match for all values.

title: Introduction
text:
Topics in This Unit
Expressions & Their Parts What expressions are made of, and how to translate short phrases into algebraic expressions (and back).
Evaluating Expressions Plug in values and simplify with the correct order of operations. See why parentheses matter.
Combining Like Terms Put “like with like” (same variable and power) to clean up expressions.
The Distributive Property Distribute to remove parentheses and simplify. Learn common slips to avoid (like trying to distribute over exponents).
Inputs, Outputs & Functions Use rules, tables, and expressions to map inputs to outputs. Decide if a relation is a function and practice simple function notation.
Equivalent Expressions Different forms, same value. Use simplification and substitution to test for equivalence, and see what counts as a proof.

title: 2.1 - Expressions & Their Parts
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
Learning mathematics is about more than number crunching, you’re learning a new language. Like any language, mathematics uses words and phrases to communicate ideas. In algebra, we call those words and phrases expressions.
In this lesson, you’ll learn to read expressions to understand the ideas they communicate and to write expressions to communicate your own ideas. To take the next step in the language of algebra, we’ll start with the basic building blocks of expressions: variables, terms, coefficients, and constants.

title: 2.2 - Evaluating Expressions
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
In the last lessons, you learned how to solve one-step and two-step equations. Those were like solving simple puzzles: one or two moves and you had the answer.
But not every equation is that neat. Sometimes parentheses get in the way, or extra terms make things look messy. These are called multi-step equations.
In this lesson, you’ll learn how to simplify first (by using the distributive property and combining like terms) and then solve the equation step by step. We’ll also practice checking our solutions to be sure they really work.

title: 2.3 - Combining Like Terms
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
When we speak, we sometimes shorten a sentence without changing its meaning. We can do the same in algebra. Expressions can be messy, so we clean them up by putting like things with like things and then adding or subtracting. This is called combining like terms.
Think of a cashier counting money in a mixed drawer. They put tens with tens, fives with fives, quarters with quarters. Once things are sorted, they’re easy to count. In algebra, we sort by the variable part and then add the coefficients.

title: 2.4 - The Distributive Property
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
Imagine your football (soccer) team wants to order new jerseys. Each jersey costs $25, and to add your team’s logo it’s another $5 per jersey.
Since there are 11 players on the team, you need 11 jerseys. You could figure out the total cost in two different ways:
First, add the cost of one jersey and the logo: 25 + 5 = 30. Then multiply by 11 → 11 × 30 = $330.
Or multiply separately: (11 × 25) + (11 × 5) = 275 + 55 = $330.
Either way, you get the same answer. What we just did actually followed a rule in algebra called the distributive property. Today, we’re going to see how this property helps us simplify expressions.

title: 2.5 - Inputs and Outputs of Functions
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
So far in this unit, you’ve learned how to evaluate expressions by plugging in values for variables. You’ve also simplified expressions using distribution and by combining like terms.
Now picture a small mystery machine on a desk with a sign that says “Feed me.” On the machine is a big letter “f” and on the table are number cards. You slide a 5 into the top, and out comes 13. You try 7, and out comes 17. When you feed the same number again, you get the same result again. It seems the machine is following a steady rule.
What could the rule be? How could we name it so others know exactly what it does? Machines like this—where each input leads to one specific output—are called functions.

title: 2.6 - Equivalent Expressions
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
When you visit another country, you might hear the same word said in different ways. Hello, hola, bonjour, all mean the same thing, but they look and sound different.
Math is like that too. An idea can be written many different ways. \(2(x+3)\) and \(2x+6\) look different, but they both “say” the same thing. We call such pairs equivalent expressions.
In this lesson, you’ll learn how to recognize when expressions are equivalent by simplifying, using substitution, and thinking logically. This idea is a big deal in Algebra, especially when we start solving equations in Unit 3.

What You’ll Learn
Welcome to Unit 3! Here we move from working with expressions to solving equations and inequalities. Instead of just simplifying or evaluating, you’ll learn how to find the value of a variable that makes an equation true. By the end of this unit, you’ll be able to:

title: Introduction
text:
Solve one-step and two-step equations by using inverse operations and check your work by substitution.

title: Introduction
text:
Topics in This Unit
Solving One-Step Equations Start small—use opposite operations to undo addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division and get the variable alone.
Solving Two-Step Equations Add or subtract first, then multiply or divide. Practice solving short, real-world problems.
Multi-Step Equations with Distribution Simplify before you solve. Distribute to remove parentheses, combine like terms, and check your solution.

title: 3.1 - Solving One-Step Equations
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
In Unit 2, we learned how to work with equivalent expressions. Sometimes we could check a number, substitute it into both expressions, and see that they matched. But, with some expressions, we noticed something important:
Some values worked.
Other values didn’t.
This brings us to equations. In this unit, we do the opposite: instead of trying numbers to check if two expressions are equal, we will learn to find the numbers that make them equal.
Those values are called the solutions of the equation.
In this lesson, we begin with the basic rules for solving equations:
Later lessons will build on these rules to solve more complicated equations.

title: 3.2 - Solving Two-Step Equations
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
With one-step equations, we identified the operation and did the opposite to both sides. Two-step equations are the same idea with one new decision to make. Which operation do we deal with first?

title: 3.2 - Solving Two-Step Equations
text:
3.2.2 - Word Problems with Two-Step Equations
Equations are especially useful when a situation involves two operations. Let’s look at some examples.

Example 4: Babysitting
A babysitter charges $10 for travel plus $8 per hour. The total charge was $42. How many hours did the babysitter work?
Let \(h\) be the number of hours worked.
The following equation can be used to model this situation.
\[
8h + 10 = 42
\]
Now we solve for \(h\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
8h + 10 \textcolor{red}{-10} &= 42 \textcolor{red}{-10} \snminus{10} \\
8h &= 32 \\
\\
8h \textcolor{red}{\div 8} &= 32 \textcolor{red}{\div 8} \sndiv{8} \\
h &= 4
\end{aligned}
\]
The babysitter worked 4 hours.

Example 5: Cellphone plan
A phone plan charges $25 each month plus $0.05 per text. Last month the bill was $32. How many texts were sent?
Let \(t\) be the number of texts sent.
The equation we use to model this is:
\[
0.05t + 25 = 32
\]
Now we solve for \(t\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
0.05t + 25 \textcolor{red}{-25} &= 32 \textcolor{red}{-25} \snminus{25} \\
0.05t &= 7 \\
\\
0.05t \textcolor{red}{\div 0.05} &= 7 \textcolor{red}{\div 0.05} \sndiv{0.05} \\
t &= 140
\end{aligned}
\]
There were 140 texts sent.

Example 6: Connections to geometry
The perimeter of a rectangle is 28cm. The length is 2 more than twice the width. Find the width of the rectangle.
Let \(W\) be the width of the rectangle.





An equation that models this situation is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
2W + 2L &= 28 \stepnote{perimeter formula} \\
\\
2W + 2(2W + 2) &= 28 \stepnote{substitute and simplify}\\
2W + 4W + 4 &= 28 \\
\\
6W + 4 &= 28
\end{aligned}
\]
Now we can solve for \(W\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
6W + 4 \textcolor{red}{-4} &= 28 \textcolor{red}{-4} \snminus{4} \\
6W &= 24 \\
\\
6W \textcolor{red}{\div 6} &= 24 \textcolor{red}{\div 6} \sndiv{6} \\
W &= 4
\end{aligned}
\]
The width of the rectangle is 4cm.

A gym membership is $20 plus $15 per class. Your total cost was $65. How many classes did you attend?


Let \(c\) be the number of classes attended.
The equation \(15c + 20 = 65\) can be used to model this situation.
\[
\begin{aligned}
15c + 20 \textcolor{red}{-20} &= 65 \textcolor{red}{-20} \snminus{20} \\
15c &= 45 \\
\\
15c \textcolor{red}{\div 15} &= 45 \textcolor{red}{\div 15} \sndiv{15} \\
c &= 3
\end{aligned}
\]
You attended 3 classes.

title: 3.3 - Multi-Step Equations with Distribution
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
In the last lessons, you learned how to solve one-step and two-step equations. Those were like solving simple puzzles: one or two moves and you had the answer.
But not every equation is that neat. Sometimes parentheses get in the way, or extra terms make things look messy. These are called multi-step equations.
In this lesson, you’ll learn how to simplify first (by using the distributive property and combining like terms) and then solve the equation step by step. We’ll also practice checking our solutions to be sure they really work.

title: 3.4 - Solving Equations With Variables on Both Sides
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
So far, every equation we solved had the variable on one side only. That made it clear where to “aim” our work, get the variable by itself on that side. But in real problems, equations aren’t always so neat. Sometimes the variable shows up on both sides of the equal sign.
In this lesson, you’ll learn how to bring all the variable terms together, simplify what’s left, and then solve.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\textcolor{red}{3}(x - 7) &= 3 \\
3x - 21 &= 3 \\
\\
3x - 21 \textcolor{red}{+ 21} &= 3 \\
3x &= 3 \\
\\
3x \textcolor{red}{\div 3} &= 3 \textcolor{red}{\div 3} \\
x &= 1
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 3.4 - Solving Equations With Variables on Both Sides
section: 3.4.3 - Word Problems with Variables on Both Sides
text:
3.4.3 - Word Problems with Variables on Both Sides
When two different plans or expressions both describe the same total, we often get equations with the variable on both sides. Simplify each side (distribute, combine like terms), then move all variable terms to one side.

Example 6: Two pay plans
Alex earns a $6 bonus plus $15 per hour. Blair earns a $18 bonus plus $12 per hour. After how many hours will they earn the same amount?
Let \(h\) be the number of hours.
\[
15h + 6 = 12h + 18
\]
Solve:
\[
\begin{aligned}
15h + 6 \textcolor{red}{-12h} &= 12h + 18 \textcolor{red}{-12h} \snminus{12h} \\
3h + 6 &= 18 \\
\\
3h + 6 \textcolor{red}{-6} &= 18 \textcolor{red}{-6} \snminus{6} \\
3h &= 12 \\
\\
3h \textcolor{red}{\div 3} &= 12 \textcolor{red}{\div 3} \sndiv{3} \\
h &= 4
\end{aligned}
\]
They earn the same after 4 hours.

Example 7: Equal perimeters
Two rectangles have the same perimeter.

Rectangle A: length \(x + 6\), width \(x + 2\)
Rectangle B: length \(2x - 1\), width \(x + 3\)

Find \(x\).
Perimeter: \(P = 2(\text{length} + \text{width})\).
\[
2\big((x+6) + (x+2)\big) = 2\big((2x-1) + (x+3)\big)
\]
Distribute and simplify:
\[
\begin{aligned}
2(2x + 8) &= 2(3x + 2) \stepnote{Distribute both sides} \\
4x + 16 &= 6x + 4 \\
\\
4x + 16 \textcolor{red}{- 6x} &= 6x + 4 \textcolor{red}{- 6x} \snminus{6x} \\
-2x + 16 &= 4 \\
\\
-2x + 16 \textcolor{red}{- 16} &= 4 \textcolor{red}{- 16} \snminus{16} \\
-2x &= -12 \\
\\
-2x \textcolor{red}{\div -2} &= -12 \textcolor{red}{\div -2} \sndiv{-2} \\
x &= 6
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(x = 6\).

Example 8: Two vendors, same total
Vendor A sells sweatshirts for $18 each, includes 2 free, and charges $12 shipping. Vendor B sells sweatshirts for $15 each with a flat $42 shipping. For how many sweatshirts do the totals match?
Let \(s\) be the number of sweatshirts ordered.
Vendor A total: pay for \((s-2)\) shirts (because 2 are free) and add $12 shipping
\[
18(s - 2) + 12
\]
Vendor B total: \[
15s + 42
\]
Set them equal:
\[
18(s - 2) + 12 = 15s + 42
\]
Distribute and solve:
\[
\begin{aligned}
18(s - 2) + 12 &= 15s + 42 \stepnote{Distribute the 18} \\
18s - 36 + 12 &= 15s + 42 \\
\\
18s \textcolor{blue}{- 36} \textcolor{blue}{+ 12} &= 15s + 42 \stepnote{Combine like terms} \\
18s \textcolor{blue}{- 24} &= 15s + 42 \\
\\
18s - 24 \textcolor{red}{- 15s} &= 15s + 42 \textcolor{red}{- 15s} \snminus{15s} \\
3s - 24 &= 42 \\
\\
3s - 24 \textcolor{red}{+ 24} &= 42 \textcolor{red}{+ 24} \snplus{24} \\
3s &= 66 \\
\\
3s \textcolor{red}{\div 3} &= 66 \textcolor{red}{\div 3} \sndiv{3} \\
s &= 22
\end{aligned}
\]
The totals match at 22 sweatshirts.


Plan A costs $8 per month plus $3 per premium movie. Plan B costs $2 per month plus $5 per premium movie. For how many premium movies will the plans cost the same in a month?


Let \(m\) be the number of premium movies.
\[
8 + 3m = 2 + 5m
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
8 + 3m \textcolor{red}{-5m} &= 2 + 5m \textcolor{red}{-5m} \snminus{5m} \\
8 - 2m &= 2 \\
\\
8 - 2m \textcolor{red}{-8} &= 2 \textcolor{red}{-8} \snminus{8} \\
-2m &= -6 \\
\\
-2m \textcolor{red}{\div -2} &= -6 \textcolor{red}{\div -2} \sndiv{-2} \\
m &= 3
\end{aligned}
\]
They match at 3 movies.

title: 3.5 - Equations With No or Infinite Solutions
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
So far, every equation we solved had exactly one solution. After simplifying and moving terms, we always ended with something like
\[
x=5
\]
which tells us the one value that makes the equation true.
But equations don’t always behave that way. Sometimes:
These are called special cases. In this lesson, we’ll see what they look like and how to spot them.

title: 3.6 - Solving Inequalities
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
You have $20 in your pocket and want to buy some candy at the grocery store. You need to buy bread for $3.50, and each package of candy costs $1.25. How many packages of candy can you afford?
We might try to model this problem with the following equation.
Let \(c\) be the number of packages of candy you purchase.
\[
3.5 + 1.25c = 20
\]
Solving for \(c\) gives us:
\[
\begin{aligned}
3.5 + 1.25c \textcolor{red}{-3.5} &= 20 \textcolor{red}{-3.5} \snminus{3.5} \\
1.25c &= 16.5 \\
\\
1.25c \textcolor{red}{\div 1.25} &= 16.5 \textcolor{red}{\div 1.25} \sndiv{1.25} \\
c &= 13.2
\end{aligned}
\]
This tells us you can afford 13.2 packages of candy—but you can’t just buy part of a package.
Problems like this one show the limitations of equations. Equations are great when there’s a single exact answer, but real situations often have ranges of possible answers. To describe those ranges, we use inequalities.
Unlike an equation, inequalities help us solve problems with a range of answers.

title: 3.7 - Solving Literal Equations
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
Imagine you’re asked to solve for time \(t\) in the equation \(d = rt\). You might recognize this as the distance formula: distance = rate × time.
If you know any two of these values, you can find the third, but what if you need to rearrange the formula itself? That’s what we call a literal equation.
Literal equations use letters (or “literals”) to represent variables, so solving them means isolating one variable in terms of the others.

title: Introduction
text:
What You’ll Learn
Welcome to Unit 4!
Here we take what you’ve learned about equations and bring them to life on the coordinate plane.
You’ll learn how equations like \(y = mx + b\) represent straight lines, what slope and intercept mean, and how these simple rules can model real situations—from earnings to motion to limits on spending.
You’ll also extend this idea to inequalities, showing not just one solution but entire regions of possibilities.
By the end of this unit, you’ll be able to:

title: Introduction
text:
Graph and interpret linear functions using equations like \(y = mx + b\) or \(f(x) = mx + b\).
Find and describe slope and intercepts, and explain what they mean in context.
Write equations of lines from graphs, tables, points, or real-world descriptions.
Use linear equations to model real situations, predict values, and estimate best-fit lines.
Graph linear inequalities to show ranges of possible solutions.

title: Introduction
text:
Topics in This Unit
Graphing Function Rules Use equations like \(y = 2x + 1\) as rules to generate points. Plot those points to see how linear functions make straight-line graphs.
Understanding Slope Explore slope as rate of change. Find slope from graphs or points, compare positive, negative, zero, and undefined slopes, and connect to real-world rates.
The Equation of a Line (\(y = mx + b\)) Discover how slope (\(m\)) and intercept (\(b\)) shape a line. Graph quickly from slope and intercept, and see how changing them moves the line.
Writing Linear Equations Write equations from graphs, data, or descriptions. Use slope-intercept and point-slope form, and explain what \(m\) and \(b\) mean in context.

title: 4.1 - Graphing Function Rules
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
So far, you’ve worked with rules that take an input, do something to it, and give an output. You’ve written equations, evaluated expressions, and created tables that show how numbers are connected.
In this lesson, we’ll take that same idea one step further. Instead of only listing input-output pairs, we’ll see them. Each pair becomes a point you can plot. When those points come together, they reveal a picture of the rule itself.
It’s time to move from numbers to shapes, and start seeing how a function behaves.

title: 4.2 - Understanding Slope
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
In the previous lesson, you graphed straight lines by making a table of \(x\) and \(y\) values. Different equations made different graphs, but they were all linear, their points lined up perfectly.
In real-world situations, we often want to compare how fast things change. Some lines rise quickly, some fall, and others stay flat. That rate of change is called the slope, one of the most important ideas in algebra.

title: 4.3 - The Equation of a Line
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
In the last lesson, you learned how to find and use the slope of a line. Now you’ll see how slope connects to a line’s equation, and how one special point called the y-intercept helps you write that equation quickly.
Lines are everywhere. We see them on roads, ramps, graphs of data, the list goes on and on. Every straight line can be described with just two numbers: its slope and its y-intercept. Once you know those, you can write an equation, make predictions, and see how the line behaves, all without having to graph every single point.

title: 4.4 - Writing Linear Equations
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
In the last lesson, you learned how slope and intercept describe a line. Now you’ll learn how to write the equation for a line when you’re given different kinds of information.
Every situation leads back to the same form:
\[
y = mx + b
\]
The key is to recognize what you already know (the slope, a point, or both) and use it to build the rule for your line.

title: 4.5 - Systems of Equations
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
So far, you’ve graphed one line at a time, each showing a single rule or relationship. But life isn’t always that simple.
Imagine comparing two phone plans. Each one has a different starting fee and a different rate per minute. You might wonder: When will they cost the same?
That kind of question can’t be answered with just one line, you have to see both relationships together. When two lines meet, they show a shared truth, a point that works for both situations.
That’s the idea behind a system of equations.

title: 4.6 - Linear Models in the Real World
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
Real life is full of linear patterns. Examples include pay that rises with hours worked, temperature that drops over time, or costs that increase as you buy more. In any situation where something changes at a steady rate, you can use a linear model to describe it.
You’ve already worked with many linear models in previous lessons. They all followed the pattern \(y = mx + b\).
In this lesson, you will learn how to use these linear models to solve real-world problems involving constant rates of change.

When we switch from equations to inequalities, we’re no longer looking for one line that fits. We’re looking for all the points that make the inequality true, a whole region of the graph.

What You’ll Learn
Welcome to Unit 5!
This unit brings together two big ideas in algebra: exponents and polynomials.
You’ll learn how powers behave, how polynomial expressions are built, and how to rewrite them in cleaner, more useful forms.
As you work through the lessons, you’ll move from simplifying and multiplying polynomials to factoring, which is the reverse process. Factoring becomes a major skill later in Algebra, especially when solving quadratic equations.
By the end of this unit, you’ll be able to:

text:

Rewrite and simplify polynomials by distributing and combining like terms.
Multiply polynomials with visual models and structured methods.
Factor polynomials by taking a GCF and breaking down trinomials.

title: 5.1 - Exponent Rules
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
When we start working with algebraic expressions, we quickly see powers like \(x^2\), \(x^3\), or \(x^4\). These expressions use exponents to show repeated multiplication.
Instead of writing \(x \cdot x \cdot x \cdot x\), we can write \(x^4\). This shorthand makes it much easier to work with larger problems, but it also means we need to know how powers behave when we multiply, divide, or raise them to other powers.
In this lesson, we’ll learn the rules, unpack why they work, and learn how to use them to simplify expressions.
Simplify each expression.

title: 5.2 - Simplifying Polynomials
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
In the last lesson, you learned how exponents behave: how powers multiply, divide, and combine. Now we will use those same ideas to understand and simplify polynomials, the expressions that form the backbone of algebra.
When we simplify polynomials, we are really just doing what we have always done: organize, combine, and clean things up, but now with variables and exponents.

title: 5.3 - Multiplying Polynomials
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
You already know how to multiply a single term by a polynomial, distribute and combine like terms. But once both polynomials have more than one term, things can get complicated in a hurry.
Take something like:
\[(x + 4)(x^2 - 3x + 2).\]
Every part of the first polynomial needs to connect with every part of the second. How many products does that make? And what’s the best way to organize all those pieces so nothing gets lost?
In this lesson, you’ll learn a method that keeps everything in order and works for any size polynomial. It gives you the structure you need now, and it sets up the skills we’ll use later when we start factoring.

title: 5.4 - Factoring: GCF & Basic Trinomials
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
You’ve spent a lot of time learning how to simplify expressions: distribute, combine like terms, and rewrite things in cleaner forms. But sometimes we want to go in the opposite direction.
Take something like:
\[
12x + 18.
\]
It looks simple, but there’s structure hidden inside it. Could this expression be written as a product of smaller pieces?
Now look at a trinomial such as
\[
x^2 + 11x + 24.
\]
Where did it come from? Could it be the result of multiplying two binomials? If so, how could we work backward to uncover them?
In this lesson, we will find the answers to these questions by learning the basics of factoring polynomials.

title: 5.5 - Factoring: General Trinomials & Special Patterns
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
Up until now, the trinomials you have been factoring have all started the same way. The first term has always been something like \(x^2\). That made the area model feel comfortable, because the first box always held \(x^2\) and the first terms in the factors were simply \(x\) and \(x\).
But what if the trinomial started with something like \(6x^2\) instead of \(x^2\)?
What would go in the first box then, and what would the first terms in the factors look like?
Would the same process still work?
Here is another question to think about. What if the trinomial does not fit the same product sum pattern you used before? Is there some structure hiding inside it, or is it something completely different?
These questions will guide us as we look at trinomials that do not follow the familiar patterns from earlier lessons. Some will behave in ways you expect, and others will require a new idea or two. As we explore them, the area model will continue to be our main tool, and you will see how it adapts to these new situations.

What You’ll Learn
Welcome to Unit 6!
This unit is all about quadratic functions, one of the most important and powerful ideas in Algebra. Quadratics show up whenever something rises and falls, speeds up and slows down, or reaches a highest or lowest point.
You will explore what quadratic functions look like, how to graph them, and how to solve quadratic equations in multiple ways. Each method gives you a different perspective, and together they help you understand both the structure of quadratics and how they behave.
As you move through the unit, you will go from visual ideas like graphs and symmetry to algebraic techniques like factoring, completing the square, and using the quadratic formula. By the end, you will be able to apply quadratics to real situations and interpret what the solutions actually mean.
By the end of this unit, you’ll be able to:

title: 6.1 - Introduction to Quadratics
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
Up to now, we have learned a lot about functions that model situations with straight-line behavior. Linear functions are useful in many real-world situations, but many things do not move in straight lines. One example is the path of a thrown ball.
When you throw a ball, it rises, slows down, reaches a highest point, and then falls. If you traced the path it makes in the air, the curve looks like a smooth U shape.
How could we model something like this?
In this lesson, we will learn a new type of function that can model curved paths like the one above. We call these functions quadratics.

title: 6.2 – Graphing Quadratics
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
In the last lesson, you looked at graphs of quadratic functions and learned the key features of a parabola: the vertex, the axis of symmetry, and how the graph can have a maximum or a minimum.
Earlier in the course, you graphed lines by starting with a table of values and later moved to using slope and intercept directly from the equation.
Now we ask a similar question for quadratics:
How can we use a quadratic equation to graph its parabola?

title: 6.3 - Solving Quadratic Equations by Factoring
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
In the last two lessons, we learned how to graph quadratic functions and describe the shapes of their parabolas. We now know how they open, where their vertices are, and how to find key features on the graph.
But quadratics are not just interesting curves. They also show up in equations we need to solve, like
\[
x^2 + 2x = 8.
\]
It is natural to ask how we would solve an equation like this.
In this lesson, we will see that we already have all of the tools we need.
Warm-Up

title: 6.4 - Completing the Square
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
In the last lesson, we solved quadratic equations by factoring. When a quadratic factors nicely, this method works well.
But not all quadratic equations factor using integers.
For example,
\[
x^2 + 6x + 5 = 0
\]
factors easily, while
\[
x^2 + 6x + 2 = 0
\]
does not.
Both parabolas cross the \(x\)-axis twice, so both equations have two solutions. We can find the solutions to the first equation by factoring:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2 + 6x + 5 &= 0 \\
(x + 5)(x + 1) &= 0
\end{aligned}
\]
This gives the solutions \(x = -5\) and \(x = -1\).
But factoring does not work for the second equation. We need a method that works every time, even when factoring fails.
In this lesson, we will learn a method called completing the square. This method always works for quadratic equations. What’s more, it leads directly to one of the most important formulas in algebra: the quadratic formula.
Warm-Up

title: 6.5 - The Quadratic Formula
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
By now, you’ve seen several ways to solve quadratic equations. Some factor nicely. Some can be solved using square roots. Some can be rewritten by completing the square.
But not all quadratic equations cooperate.
In this lesson, we will develop a general method that works for every quadratic equation. This method leads to a single formula that packages all of the algebra into one place: the quadratic formula.
\[
x^2 - 9 = 0
\]
\[
x^2 - 6x + 9 = 0
\]
\[
x^2 + 3x + 1 = 0
\]
What method would you normally try first? What makes this one harder than the others?

title: 6.6 - Applications of Quadratics
text:
🔥 Warm-Up
So far, we have focused on how to work with quadratic equations. We have learned how to factor them, complete the square, use square roots, and apply the quadratic formula.
But quadratic equations were not invented just to be solved.
They model real situations involving height, distance, area, revenue, and time. In this lesson, we will use quadratics to make sense of real world problems and interpret what the solutions actually mean.
